youtube_title: If a Monkey Takes the Photo, Who Owns the Copyright? 🦝⚖️
caption: The U.S. Copyright Office won't register works produced by animals — and its own rulebook lists 'a photo taken by a monkey' as an example. Owning the camera isn't the same as being the author.
script: If a monkey takes the photo, who gets the copyright? Under U.S. law, the answer is awkward. The U.S. Copyright Office has a rulebook for what it will register, called the Compendium. And it says plainly: the Office will not register works produced by nature, animals, or plants. Then it gives examples. A photo taken by a monkey. A mural painted by an elephant. Driftwood shaped and smoothed by the ocean. Even a song application that names the Holy Spirit as its author. The principle is human authorship. Copyright protects creative work by people. So imagine you set up a camera, and a monkey grabs it and snaps a picture. You may own the camera. You may own the memory card. But owning the equipment doesn't make you the author of a photo the monkey took. Here's the limit. This doesn't mean every picture with an animal in it is unprotected. A photographer who chooses the shot, the framing and the moment is a human author. When a person and an animal both play a part, the human contribution has to be looked at on its own. And this is a U.S. copyright explanation. Other countries can see things differently, and other rights, like contracts, can still matter. [loop] So the next time a monkey borrows your camera, remember
